logline: A 13-year-old boy is arrested for murdering a classmate, and four single-take episodes track a year of investigation, school corridors, therapy sessions, and a family coming apart at the seams.

renewal.note: A four-episode limited series; Jack Thorne and Stephen Graham have confirmed no Season 2.

bollymeter.basis: 100% on Rotten Tomatoes; one of the most formally audacious pieces of British television in years - every episode shot in a single unbroken take, directed by Philip Barantini, forcing an intensity of performance and presence that conventional editing would have made avoidable.

pull_quotes.text: Adolescence is quietly devastating - a formally audacious, morally serious examination of violence, boyhood, and the families left behind.

seasons.review_body: Adolescence is the 2025 television event that most precisely deserved the word 'event'. The formal conceit - every episode in a single unbroken take - was not a stunt; it was a structural necessity for a story about bearing witness without escape. Director Philip Barantini, working from Jack Thorne's writing, turned the camera into an accomplice that followed these people through a year of grief and investigation and couldn't look away. Owen Cooper's Jamie was the show's sustained miracle: a child-actor performance that critics at 100% called genuinely unprecedented. Stephen Graham, who also produced, delivered the kind of work that makes other actors' careers look comfortable. Netflix reported staggering opening-week viewership. The four-episode structure meant the show ended before it could outstay itself.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Adolescence Episode 1 announces its formal commitment immediately: the entire episode is a single unbroken shot. Not an aesthetic stunt but a structural argument - the refusal to cut refuses the audience the small cognitive rest that editing provides, forcing attention into the same duration as the people being followed. The episode opens before dawn, a door broken down, a 13-year-old taken from his family home in handcuffs. The camera follows Jamie Miller and his father through the police station - interview rooms, corridors, waiting areas, the mechanics of arrest - without relief or perspective-shift. Owen Cooper's performance as Jamie is the formal gamble's vindication: a 13-year-old face on which accusation, fear, and something harder to name play out in a space where the camera cannot look away. Stephen Graham as the father provides the adult register - a man trying to understand something that does not yield to parental understanding. The episode was created by Jack Thorne (writing) and directed by Philip Barantini (who developed the one-shot feature 'Boiling Point'). Its 100% RT debut is the expected critical response to a piece of television that is technically near-impossible and emotionally devastating.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A door broken down before dawn. A 13-year-old taken from his home in handcuffs. The entire police station sequence - interview rooms, corridors, waiting areas - follows Jamie and his father in a single unbroken shot that refuses to let the camera rest anywhere easier. By the episode's end, a question has been posed that the remaining three hours will circle without ever quite answering cleanly.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The interview room scene - Jamie's face when the accusation lands, held in one uncut take.

critic_note.text: Adolescence Episode 1 is the most formally startling British television debut in years.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 3
episode_reviews.review_body: Adolescence Episode 3 is the show's formal and dramatic peak: one unbroken shot, one room, a teenage boy and a psychologist. The episode runs approximately 50 minutes and holds two people in a space from which the camera never departs. Erin Doherty as Dr. Briony Ariston approaches Jamie with the patience of a trained clinician and the intelligence of a writer who has thought carefully about what trauma conceals and how it conceals itself. Owen Cooper's performance in this episode is the one that critics referenced when discussing Adolescence as an all-time achievement: a child dismantling his own defenses and then dismantling the defenses of his defenses, the camera present for the whole process. The structural choice - one continuous take, one room, no external reference points - strips away every narrative device that usually mediates the audience's relationship with a difficult subject. What surfaces in this episode is not resolution; it is something more unsettling, and more honest. The RT consensus called it one of the most accomplished pieces of two-person television drama ever made, and the claim is defensible.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Jamie meets with a psychologist. One room, two people, one continuous hour. The episode is a chamber piece that slowly dismantles the child's defenses - and then the defenses' defenses - until something that might be truth surfaces. Critics isolated this episode as the performance peak of the entire series.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The moment the psychologist reaches something in Jamie that the police interviews couldn't - the pivot the whole show turns on.

critic_note.text: Episode 3 of Adolescence is one of the most accomplished pieces of two-person television drama ever made.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 4
episode_reviews.review_body: The Adolescence finale follows Eddie Miller - the father - through a single day. The choice to close the series on the parent rather than the child is the show's final structural argument: this is not ultimately a story about what Jamie did but about what a family becomes afterwards. The episode is, like all four, a single unbroken shot. Stephen Graham's performance - a father maintaining the physical motions of a birthday celebration inside a home that has permanently changed shape - operates at a register where craft becomes invisible, where the tools disappear and what remains is simply a person in a situation the camera has been trusted to carry. The birthday cake sequence, identified by multiple critics as the episode's central image, functions as the show's thematic summary: ordinary love persisting inside extraordinary devastation, not as consolation but as fact. The RT consensus noted that the finale 'trusts its audience to do the emotional mathematics,' which is the correct description of a finale that withholds the catharsis a lesser series would supply. Adolescence concludes as one of the defining British television achievements of the 2020s.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Eddie Miller's birthday. The family attempts normalcy inside a house that no longer has a structure that supports normalcy. Stephen Graham's performance here reaches something beyond craft - a father trying to hold the shape of a family that the shape no longer fits. The final minutes land with accumulated weight.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The birthday cake - an act of love so ordinary inside circumstances so extraordinary it breaks differently than any explicit scene could.

critic_note.text: The Adolescence finale trusts its audience to do the emotional mathematics - a rare and correct choice.
